chapter_summary:
Building upon our understanding of Direct Connect's purpose, let's now dissect its architecture and the critical components that make it function. A Direct Connect setup isn't just a single cable; it's an intricate orchestration of physical infrastructure and logical configurations that bridge your on-premises network with the vast AWS global network. Understanding these components is vital for designing, implementing, and troubleshooting your hybrid connectivity.

At the heart of the physical setup is the **Direct Connect location**. These are colocation facilities or carrier hotels strategically distributed globally, where AWS has deployed its network equipment. These locations serve as the physical demarcation point between your network and AWS. When you order a Direct Connect connection, you'll select a DX location close to your data center or office. This proximity is crucial for minimizing the "last mile" latency between your premises and the AWS network. Within these locations, AWS maintains dedicated routers and switches, ready to receive your connection.

Your journey to connect to AWS begins with establishing a **cross-connect**. A cross-connect is a physical cable (typically fiber optic) that runs from your network device (or your colocation provider's device) within the Direct Connect location to the AWS Direct Connect router. This is the actual physical link that carries your traffic. To facilitate this, you must obtain a **Letter of Authorization – Connecting Facility Assignment (LOA-CFA)** from AWS. The LOA-CFA is a critical document that authorizes your colocation provider to establish the cross-connect on your behalf. It contains specific details like the AWS port ID, the patch panel information, and the required cable type. Without a valid LOA-CFA, your colocation provider cannot physically connect your equipment to AWS. This document is typically generated automatically when you create a new Direct Connect connection in the AWS console and must be provided to your colocation provider within a specific timeframe (usually 90 days) before it expires. Failing to provide this in time or providing incorrect details are common pitfalls that can significantly delay your connection.

Once the cross-connect is established, the physical layer is complete. The next step involves configuring the logical layer, which primarily revolves around **Virtual Interfaces (VIFs)**. A VIF is a logical connection created on top of your physical Direct Connect link. It allows you to access different types of AWS services. We'll delve deeper into VIFs in a later chapter, but it's important to know now that you can have multiple VIFs over a single physical Direct Connect connection, enabling you to segregate traffic for different purposes (e.g., private access to VPCs, public access to S3, or transit gateway connectivity). Each VIF requires BGP peering, where your on-premises router exchanges routing information with the AWS Direct Connect router. Your router acts as the **customer gateway (CGW)** in this context, providing the on-premises endpoint for the BGP session.

The AWS side of the connection involves a **Direct Connect connection** resource, which you provision in the AWS console. This resource represents the physical port on the AWS router. When you create this, you specify the Direct Connect location, the port speed (e.g., 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps), and whether it's a dedicated or hosted connection. Associated with this Direct Connect connection are the **Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)** or **Transit Gateway (TGW)** for private VIFs, which serve as the AWS endpoint for your VPCs. For public VIFs, the traffic is routed directly to the public AWS network. Understanding the interplay between these components is crucial. The physical connection (cross-connect) provides the raw bandwidth, the LOA-CFA enables the physical connection, the Direct Connect connection resource manages the AWS port, and VIFs provide the logical paths to AWS services, all orchestrated by BGP for dynamic routing. Always ensure your on-premises router configuration, including BGP ASN, IP addresses, and VLAN IDs, precisely matches the configuration provided by AWS for your VIFs to avoid connectivity issues.

```bash
# Example BGP configuration snippet for an on-premises Cisco router
# This is illustrative and will vary based on your router and AWS VIF details.

router bgp <YOUR_ONPREM_ASN>
 bgp log-neighbor-changes
 neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> remote-as <AWS_BGP_ASN>
 neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> description AWS_DirectConnect_Peer
 neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> password <BGP_AUTH_KEY_FROM_AWS>
 !
 address-family ipv4
  network <YOUR_ONPREM_NETWORK_PREFIX> mask <YOUR_ONPREM_NETWORK_MASK>
  neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> activate
  neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> soft-reconfiguration inbound
 exit-address-family
```
This snippet shows how you would configure BGP on your router to peer with the AWS Direct Connect router. The `YOUR_ONPREM_ASN` is your Autonomous System Number, `AWS_BGP_IP` is the IP address AWS assigns for its BGP peer, and `AWS_BGP_ASN` is the AWS ASN (usually 64512 for private VIFs). The `BGP_AUTH_KEY` is a crucial shared secret for authentication. Incorrect BGP configuration is a very common mistake during DX setup, leading to routes not being exchanged and connectivity failures. Always double-check these parameters against the AWS console's VIF configuration details.

screens.title: Direct Connect Components and Architecture
screens.subtitle: From the rack to BGP: the physical and logical pieces that make a Direct Connect link function

narration.text: In this lesson we will map the complete chain from your on-premises router to the AWS network, and explain why each step matters. You will learn what a Direct Connect location is, how a cross-connect physically links your equipment to AWS, and why the LOA-CFA document is a required authorization. We'll also cover the logical layer: Direct Connect connection resources, virtual interfaces, and BGP peering to exchange routes. Understanding these parts helps you design reliable low-latency hybrid networks and speeds troubleshooting when issues occur. For example, a mismatch between the VLAN ID declared in the AWS VIF details and the one configured on your router will block traffic even if the fiber is active. The goal here is practical: after this lesson you can identify the physical demarcation, gather the correct data for a colocation provider, and verify the essential on‑prem router settings needed for a healthy BGP session. A common mistake to avoid is treating the LOA-CFA as optional; it is the formal authorization for the facility to provision the fiber. As you go through the screens, notice the recurring theme: a physical object is paired with a logical configuration, and both must match precisely. Keep that question in mind: what piece would I check first when a Direct Connect circuit shows no routes?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Direct Connect combines physical infrastructure (location, cross-connect, LOA-CFA) with logical resources (connection, VIFs, BGP) and both layers must be correct for connectivity.

screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify and describe the core physical and logical pieces of an AWS Direct Connect setup and explain how they fit together. First, you should clearly name the Direct Connect location, the cross-connect fiber, and the AWS router port as the physical demarcation. Second, you will understand the LOA-CFA: what it contains, why a colocation provider needs it, and the operational impact of an expired or incorrect LOA-CFA. Third, you should recognize how a Direct Connect connection resource represents an AWS port with a chosen speed and connection type. Fourth, you will be able to explain virtual interfaces and the need for BGP peering with your customer gateway, plus why matching ASN, IPs, and VLAN IDs matters. Each objective links a technical action to practical value — for example, collecting LOA-CFA details ahead of time keeps installation windows on schedule. Throughout the objectives you will practice spotting common mistakes, and you will leave ready to prepare a colocation provider packet and validate basic router configuration before a cutover.

keyIdea.text: Gather LOA-CFA details, confirm physical port parameters, and verify matching BGP/VLAN settings to ensure a successful Direct Connect deployment.

narration.text: This second objectives slide shifts from identification to preparation and verification. You should be able to generate and inspect the LOA-CFA for the port ID, patch panel location, cable type and expiration date and understand why those details are required by a colocation provider. You will also learn to choose an appropriate Direct Connect location and port speed, weighing proximity to your data center to reduce last-mile latency. Another key objective is configuring the AWS Direct Connect connection resource correctly—picking dedicated or hosted connections and noting the port speed influences the capacity available to VIFs. Finally, you'll be able to plan how to provision multiple VIFs on one physical link and prepare the on-premises router with matching BGP parameters. A practical example: when scheduling the facility install, deliver the LOA-CFA PDF with the correct port ID and confirm the expiration window to avoid reordering. These preparatory steps prevent delays and help you coordinate the physical and logical cutover with your networking team.

screens.title: Direct Connect Location — the physical demarcation point
screens.subtitle: What a DX location is and why proximity matters

narration.text: A Direct Connect location is a colocation facility or carrier hotel where AWS places its routers and switches. Think of it as the physical demarcation between your network and AWS’s network fabric. When you choose a Direct Connect location you are picking where your fiber will terminate on the AWS side; proximity reduces the length of the last mile from your data center and so reduces latency and potential last-mile faults. The location contains racks and ports that AWS manages; a Direct Connect connection maps to a physical port at that location. In practice you will choose a location that balances distance to your site, available port speeds, and the operational model of the colocation provider. A misconception is to assume any nearby facility will work the same — different Direct Connect locations may have different availability, port types, and partner arrangements. For example, if your data center is in a campus four miles from one location and two miles from another, the closer one usually gives lower latency and simpler cabling. The takeaway: treat the Direct Connect location as an essential design decision, not just a checkbox. When planning, confirm which AWS routers and ports are available at the chosen location and coordinate with the colocation team early to reserve rack space and an install window.

keyIdea.title: Location matters
keyIdea.text: Selecting the right Direct Connect location reduces last-mile latency and simplifies physical installation logistics.

screens.title: Cross-Connect: establishing the physical fiber link
screens.subtitle: How the fiber runs from your equipment to the AWS router

narration.text: A cross-connect is the physical fiber cable that connects your equipment in the Direct Connect location to the AWS Direct Connect router. The process begins after you create a Direct Connect connection in the AWS console and obtain the LOA-CFA. With that document in hand you provide it to the colocation provider, who uses the LOA-CFA details — such as the AWS port ID and patch panel info — to provision the fiber. The cross-connect itself is typically a fiber optic cable that terminates into the patch panel at both the customer and AWS racks. A practical example: you might hand the LOA-CFA PDF to the facility operator; they will identify the AWS port and run a fiber jumper from your cage to that port. Common mistakes include providing an expired LOA-CFA, which prevents the provider from proceeding, or specifying the wrong cable type so the terminations don't match. To prevent those problems validate the patch panel ID, port ID, and cable type, and check the LOA-CFA expiration window before scheduling an install. The key operational step is authorization and accurate details — the fiber runs only when the facility has both permission and precise port data. As a final check, plan an acceptance test to confirm link light and perform basic IP-level validation once BGP is configured.

keyIdea.title: Physical link steps
keyIdea.text: Provide a valid LOA-CFA to the provider, confirm port and patch panel details, and verify cable type and expiration before scheduling the cross-connect.

screens.title: Letter of Authorization — Connecting Facility Assignment (LOA-CFA)
screens.subtitle: What the LOA-CFA contains and why it is required

narration.text: The LOA-CFA is an authorization document generated by AWS when you create a Direct Connect connection. It authorizes the colocation provider to establish the physical cross-connect to a specific AWS port. Key fields you will rely on are the AWS port ID, the patch panel and rack identifiers, the suggested cable type, and the expiration date. These details are not cosmetic — the port ID tells the provider which AWS router port to wire to, the patch panel information shows the termination point, and the cable type must match the terminations on both ends. A common operational misunderstanding is to think the LOA-CFA is permanent. In reality it expires after a window, usually 90 days, and handing over an expired LOA-CFA will prevent the provider from provisioning the cross-connect. Another practical pitfall is transcription errors: a single wrong digit in a port ID can mean the fiber is patched to the wrong port. A simple verification routine prevents these failures: open the LOA-CFA PDF, confirm the port ID against the console, check the cable type and notes, and validate the expiry before sending it to the provider. In short, the LOA-CFA is both permission and instruction — treat it as a required operational artifact for any physical installation.

keyIdea.title: LOA-CFA purpose
keyIdea.text: The LOA-CFA authorizes the facility to install the cross-connect and carries the precise port and patch details the provider needs.

screens.title: Direct Connect Connection Resource and Port Options
screens.subtitle: What the connection resource represents and how port speed and type matter

narration.text: When you provision a Direct Connect connection in the AWS console you create a connection resource that represents a physical port on the AWS router at the selected DX location. You specify the location and the port speed, such as 1 Gbps or 10 Gbps, and select whether the connection is dedicated or hosted. The port speed dictates the raw bandwidth available for all virtual interfaces layered on that port. A critical practical point is that multiple VIFs can share the same physical connection, but they must fit within the capacity you ordered. A common error is undersizing the port speed relative to aggregated workloads, which forces you to either use multiple physical connections or implement traffic controls. Another operational distinction is dedicated versus hosted connections: dedicated connections map to a single customer port provisioned by AWS, while hosted connections are provisioned by an AWS partner and may have different operational workflows. The most important checks before ordering are: verify available speeds at the chosen location, consider whether a hosted partner better matches procurement constraints, and plan VIF allocation so that important services receive sufficient bandwidth. In short, treat the Direct Connect connection resource as a capacity and administrative object that must be sized and mapped to your logical design.

keyIdea.title: Connection = port + capacity
keyIdea.text: A Direct Connect connection maps to an AWS physical port with chosen speed and type; plan capacity and VIF allocation accordingly.

screens.title: Virtual Interfaces (VIFs): logical channels over the physical link
screens.subtitle: How VIFs separate traffic and map to AWS services

narration.text: Virtual Interfaces, or VIFs, are logical constructs that operate above the physical Direct Connect port and carry segregated traffic to different AWS endpoints. You can create multiple VIFs on a single physical connection, enabling separate logical paths for private VPC access, public AWS service access, and transit gateway connectivity. Each VIF requires its own VLAN and BGP session so traffic remains isolated and routing is exchanged independently. A practical example: you might create a private VIF for direct VPC access and a public VIF to reach S3 endpoints; both use the same fiber but appear as distinct interfaces to AWS and your router. A common misconception is thinking that one VIF can reach all services automatically — the VIF type and associated AWS endpoint determine reachability. Implementing VIFs correctly requires precise BGP and VLAN details from the AWS console; mismatched VLAN IDs or BGP ASNs will prevent peering. Plan your VIF layout with traffic segregation, security, and route policies in mind. Finally, remember that while logical separation helps with organization and security, capacity planning still depends on the underlying port speed, so allocate bandwidth and set expectations for performance across VIFs.

keyIdea.title: VIFs isolate traffic
keyIdea.text: VIFs create logical channels over a single physical port; each requires VLAN and BGP settings and maps to specific AWS endpoints.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Virtual Interfaces (VIFs)
What VIFs do
Logical interfaces that run over a physical Direct Connect port and separate traffic types.
Types of VIFs
Private VIFs for VPCs, public VIFs for AWS public services, and transit VIFs for TGW connectivity.
VLAN and BGP requirements
Each VIF uses a VLAN and requires a BGP peering session with the AWS router.
Capacity note
Multiple VIFs share the physical port’s bandwidth; plan VIF capacity against port speed.
Concrete example
Create a private VIF for VPC routing and a public VIF for S3 access. Assign distinct VLANs and configure BGP peerings so routes do not mix.
Key Takeaway

VIFs provide logical separation; ensure VLAN and BGP parameters match the AWS-provided configuration.

screens.title: BGP Peering and the Customer Gateway (CGW)
screens.subtitle: How your on-prem router peers with AWS and what can go wrong

narration.text: BGP peering is the logical mechanism by which routing information flows between your on-premises router, known in AWS terms as the customer gateway, and the AWS Direct Connect router. Establishing BGP requires precise parameters: your ASN, the AWS peer IP address, the AWS ASN for the session, the BGP authentication key if provided, and the correct VLAN ID for the VIF. The outcome is dynamic route exchange, which is far more flexible than static routes and enables automatic route propagation when you attach VPCs to VGW or TGW. A common misconception is that fiber alone ensures reachability — in practice, incorrect BGP settings will lead to an active physical link but no route exchange. For example, if your router uses the wrong remote-as value, the BGP session never forms and no prefixes are learned. A concrete troubleshooting approach is to first verify physical link light, then confirm VLAN configuration, check that peer IPs match the AWS VIF details, ensure the ASN values align, and validate the BGP authentication key if used. Below you will also find an illustrative BGP configuration snippet; use it as a template but replace placeholders with the exact values from your AWS VIF details. End with this question: if you have link light but no BGP adjacency, which three parameters will you verify first? That checklist will save you time during cutover.

keyIdea.title: BGP checklist
keyIdea.text: Verify VLAN, peer IPs and ASN values first when a physical link is up but routes are not exchanged.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › BGP Peering & Customer Gateway
BGP peering essentials
Your on-prem router (CGW) peers with the AWS Direct Connect router using BGP for dynamic route exchange.
Required parameters
Local ASN, AWS ASN, peer IPs, VLAN ID, and optional BGP auth key.
Common error
Incorrect ASN or peer IP prevents adjacency even when the fiber is active.
Key Takeaway

If link light is present but no routes are learned, first verify VLAN, ASN and peer IPs.

Illustrative BGP config
# Example BGP configuration snippet for an on-premises Cisco router
# Replace placeholders with values from the AWS VIF details.
router bgp <YOUR_ONPREM_ASN>
 bgp log-neighbor-changes
 neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> remote-as <AWS_BGP_ASN>
 neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> description AWS_DirectConnect_Peer
 neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> password <BGP_AUTH_KEY_FROM_AWS>
 !
 address-family ipv4
  network <YOUR_ONPREM_NETWORK_PREFIX> mask <YOUR_ONPREM_NETWORK_MASK>
  neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> activate
  neighbor <AWS_BGP_IP> soft-reconfiguration inbound
 exit-address-family
Use the exact AWS VIF values for peer IP, ASNs and any authentication keys. Misconfiguration here causes route absence even when physical connectivity exists.

screens.title: VGW vs TGW and VIF Routing Targets
screens.subtitle: How private VIFs connect to VPCs and when to use a Transit Gateway

narration.text: Private virtual interfaces terminate on either a Virtual Private Gateway or a Transit Gateway depending on your design. A VGW is tied to a specific VPC and is the traditional endpoint for a private VIF, providing a direct path into that VPC’s route table. A Transit Gateway acts as a central hub that connects multiple VPCs and on-premises networks; when you need to connect many VPCs or scale hub-and-spoke routing, a TGW becomes the more scalable choice. The private VIF will peer with the AWS endpoint appropriate to your architecture and carry routes to the attached VPCs via the selected gateway. A common misconception is that private VIFs automatically connect to all VPCs — they only attach where the VGW or TGW routing is configured. For a concrete example: if you have three VPCs that must communicate with on-premises networks, attaching them to a TGW and using a private VIF to the TGW simplifies route management compared to provisioning separate VGWs. Considerations include scale, cost, and route propagation requirements. Always map your VIF type to the intended AWS endpoint when planning and verify that route tables and propagation settings on VGW or TGW align with your connectivity goals.

keyIdea.title: Routing endpoint choice
keyIdea.text: Use VGW for single-VPC private connections and TGW as a hub when connecting multiple VPCs and on-premises networks at scale.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › VGW vs TGW
Choose the right AWS endpoint
VGW attaches to a single VPC; TGW provides a hub for many VPCs and on-premises connections.
Virtual Private Gateway (VGW)
Good for single-VPC direct attachments and simpler routing models.
Transit Gateway (TGW)
Use when you need centralized routing among many VPCs and on-prem networks.
Scenario
If three VPCs need shared access to on-premises services, attach them to a Transit Gateway and use a private VIF to the TGW. If a single VPC requires direct connectivity, a VGW may suffice.
Key Takeaway

Match private VIF endpoints to your scaling needs: VGW for simple setups, TGW for hub-and-spoke scale.

screens.title: On-Premises Router Configuration Checklist
screens.subtitle: Essential parameters to match the AWS VIF settings

narration.text: Configuring the on-premises router for Direct Connect requires careful matching of the parameters AWS provides for each VIF. First, set the correct VLAN ID on the subinterface that maps to the VIF; a VLAN mismatch is an immediate blocker. Next, configure BGP with your local ASN and the AWS peer IP as the neighbor, and set the AWS ASN as the remote-as. If AWS provides a BGP authentication key, configure the same password on your neighbor definition. Assign the IP addressing as shown in the VIF details; incorrect peer IPs yield a failed adjacency. Also ensure network statements or prefix advertisements reflect the on-premises networks you intend to announce. An illustrative verification sequence after configuration is: confirm the physical link and VLAN tagging, verify the interface IPs, check BGP neighbor status for adjacency, and ensure routes are exchanged. A common mistake is partial configuration—someone may configure the ASN but forget the peer IP or auth key. For a concrete example, if AWS lists a peer IP of 192.0.2.2 and remote ASN 64512, you must use those exact values. Finally, always cross-check against the AWS console VIF details and be ready to re-run the LOA-CFA generation if any physical port changes are required.

keyIdea.title: Router verification
keyIdea.text: Confirm VLAN, peer IPs, ASN values and auth keys exactly as provided in the VIF details before attempting BGP adjacency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › On-Prem Router Checklist
Essential router parameters
Follow this checklist to avoid common cutover failures.
VLAN ID and subinterface
Match the VLAN assigned to the VIF exactly on your subinterface.
Peer IPs and ASNs
Configure neighbor with the AWS peer IP and remote-as value provided by AWS.
BGP authentication
If AWS provides a BGP auth key, set the same password on the neighbor definition.
Verification steps

  2. Check neighbor IPs and ASN match AWS VIF details.
  3. Validate BGP adjacency and route exchange.
Pro Tip

Document the exact console-provided values and paste them into your router config to avoid manual transcription errors.

screens.title: Preparing the colocation packet — a guided walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Collect the LOA-CFA and deliver the right information to your provider

narration.text: This practical walkthrough helps you prepare the colocation packet that the facility needs to install the cross-connect. Begin by creating a Direct Connect connection in the console up to the point where the LOA-CFA is generated; you do not need to finalize an order to view the LOA-CFA. Download the LOA-CFA PDF and open it to capture the port ID, patch panel location, suggested cable type, and the expiration date. Next, assemble a single packet for the colocation provider containing the LOA-CFA, a cover note with your contact and scheduling window, and the physical location details for your cage or equipment. Verify the LOA-CFA port ID against the console to avoid transcription errors. A useful practice is to include a short checklist in the packet listing the port ID, patch panel, cable type, and LOA-CFA expiration. If an expiration is approaching, regenerate a fresh LOA-CFA before submitting to the provider. Finally, plan an acceptance test after installation: confirm link light, then validate BGP adjacency and route exchange. A common real‑world consequence of skipping steps is an aborted install that wastes scheduled facility time. The core question to keep in mind is: have I given the provider exact port, patch and cable details plus an unexpired authorization?

keyIdea.title: Prepare the packet
keyIdea.text: Provide LOA-CFA, clear contact and scheduling info, and a short verification checklist so the provider can install the cross-connect reliably.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Colocation Packet Walkthrough
Step-by-step packet assembly
Follow these steps to hand the provider a complete, accurate package.
Generate LOA-CFA
Create the connection in AWS to produce the LOA-CFA PDF and capture its fields.
Assemble packet
Include LOA-CFA, contact details, scheduling window, and a checklist of port and patch IDs.
Verify and submit
Confirm LOA-CFA has sufficient expiry and send to the colocation provider as a single package.
Packet contents
  • LOA-CFA PDF (port ID, patch panel, cable type, expiry)
  • Contact and scheduling window
  • Acceptance test plan (link light, BGP adjacency, route check)
Key Takeaway

A complete packet and pre-checks prevent wasted install windows and speed up the cross-connect provisioning.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting approach
screens.subtitle: A systematic way to find the source of connectivity failures

narration.text: When a Direct Connect circuit does not pass traffic, follow a structured troubleshooting approach that separates physical and logical causes. Begin with the physical layer: confirm the cross-connect is present, that the fiber shows link light, and that the port and patch panel IDs match the LOA-CFA and console. If the physical layer is healthy, move to the VLAN and subinterface tagging on your router — a mismatched VLAN prevents the AWS VIF from seeing traffic. Next verify BGP: check neighbor status, ensure your ASN and the AWS ASN match the VIF details, and confirm the peer IPs and any authentication key. Also confirm that the VIF type maps to the intended AWS endpoint — for example, a private VIF will not provide direct public AWS service routes. Common mistakes include expired LOA-CFAs, transcription errors in port IDs, incorrect VLAN tags, and wrong ASN values. A concrete example: a fiber installed to the wrong port will show link light but AWS will not see your traffic — verifying port IDs against the LOA-CFA quickly exposes that problem. End each troubleshooting session by documenting the discovery and corrective step so the next cutover benefits from lessons learned. The guiding question: which layer failed — physical, data link (VLAN), or network (BGP)?

keyIdea.title: Systematic troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Check physical link and port IDs first, then VLAN/tagging, then BGP parameters to isolate the failure quickly.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting
A layered troubleshooting checklist
Separate checks by physical, data link and network layers to find root causes efficiently.
Layer 1 — Physical
Link light, correct port ID, and correct patch panel per LOA-CFA.
Layer 2 — VLAN
Confirm subinterface tagging and VLAN ID match the VIF configuration.
Layer 3 — BGP
Verify ASN values, peer IPs, authentication keys, and route advertisements.
Common failures
  • Expired LOA-CFA preventing provisioning.
  • Transcription errors in port or patch IDs.
  • Mismatched VLAN or wrong ASN on the router.
Remember

A healthy physical layer with incorrect logical settings will still fail; always validate both sides.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's review the three most important concepts from this chapter. First, the Direct Connect location is the physical demarcation where AWS equipment lives; selecting the right location affects latency and installation. Second, the LOA-CFA is a required authorization and the instruction set for the colocation provider; verify its port ID, patch panel details, cable type and expiration before handing it off. Third, virtual interfaces and BGP form the logical layer; each VIF needs a VLAN and a BGP session with matching ASNs and peer IPs to exchange routes. Keep in mind the operational pattern: physical authorization and cabling must align with accurate logical configuration. If any single piece is incorrect — an expired LOA-CFA, mismatched VLAN, or wrong ASN — connectivity fails. Carry these checks into your planning and you will reduce installation surprises and debugging time.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Physical and logical components must match precisely: location, LOA-CFA, cross-connect, connection resource, VIFs and BGP settings.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts
Direct Connect Location
The physical facility housing AWS routers where cross-connects terminate.
LOA-CFA
Authorization document with port ID, patch and cable details required by the facility.
VIFs & BGP
Logical interfaces using VLANs and BGP to carry routes to AWS endpoints.
Summary takeaway
Treat the Direct Connect setup as paired physical and logical tasks: secure proper authorization and cabling, then mirror those details in your VIF and BGP configuration to enable route exchange.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you implement Direct Connect

narration.text: As a quick reference before you implement, keep these three reminders close. One: the LOA-CFA is essential and time-limited; generate and provide a current LOA-CFA with accurate port and patch details. Two: multiple virtual interfaces can share one physical port, but VLAN IDs and BGP sessions must be configured correctly for each VIF. Three: validate BGP parameters — local ASN, AWS ASN, and peer IPs — and confirm any authentication key to establish adjacency. These reminders cover authorization, logical separation, and routing correctness. Carry them into your planning and install checklist to reduce the chance of delays or misconfigurations during cutover. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: LOA-CFA validity, VIF/VLAN mapping, and accurate BGP parameters are the three pillars for a successful Direct Connect deployment.

LOA-CFA validity
Always check expiration and port/patch accuracy before sending to the provider.
VIF and VLAN mapping
Assign separate VLANs and VIFs for private, public and transit traffic as needed.
Accurate BGP parameters
Match ASN, peer IPs and auth keys to the AWS VIF details to form adjacency.
Final takeaway
Successful Direct Connect setups pair correct physical authorizations and cabling with precisely matching logical configurations. Verify both to ensure a smooth cutover.
